title: Phaedrus
author: Plato
openingText: SOCRATES: My dear Phaedrus, where are you coming from, and where are you going?
about:
Socrates and Phaedrus leave Athens and sit beside the river Ilissus to talk about love. Phaedrus reads a speech by Lysias; Socrates answers with two speeches of his own. His account of the soul as a charioteer with two winged horses turns the conversation toward beauty, desire and the pursuit of truth.

The speakers then examine their speeches: What makes an argument convincing, and does a persuasive speaker need to know the truth? Their discussion ends with the limits of writing and the possibilities of a living conversation. The dialogue presents ancient views of desire, social roles and the soul; its myths and claims are invitations to examine the argument, not descriptions of established science.

angleCards.title: Why does Socrates change his mind?
angleCards.text: His first speech criticizes the lover; his second praises a form of love as divine inspiration. Compare the definitions and assumptions that make each argument possible.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the change between Socrates's two speeches and test the reasons he gives.

angleCards.title: The soul as a chariot
angleCards.text: A charioteer struggles to guide two very different horses. Follow the details of the image and ask what it explains about desire, self-control and memory.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the chariot myth and consider both the strengths and the limits of its account of inner conflict.

angleCards.title: Persuasion and truth
angleCards.text: Socrates examines speechwriting techniques, then asks what a speaker must know about the subject and the listener. Compare technical skill with the fuller understanding he demands.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the relationship between persuasive speech, truth and understanding an audience.

angleCards.title: Can a text answer back?
angleCards.text: The story of Theuth and Thamus questions whether writing strengthens memory and understanding. Consider how this written dialogue asks its reader to think beyond the words on the page.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test the critique of writing and compare reading with learning through conversation.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: Phaedrus's companion for the walk. He delivers two contrasting speeches about love and then examines what makes speaking and writing worthwhile.

cast.name: Phaedrus
cast.description: An admirer of speeches who brings Lysias's text with him. His questions and responses help the conversation move from love to rhetoric and writing.

cast.name: The charioteer and horses
cast.description: In Socrates's myth, a charioteer drives two winged horses with conflicting tendencies. Their struggle connects desire and self-control with the soul's recollection of beauty.

cast.name: Lysias
cast.description: His speech argues that someone who is not in love is a better partner than someone who is. Phaedrus reads it aloud; Socrates later examines its assumptions and structure.

cast.name: Theuth and Thamus
cast.role: Figures in the story of writing
cast.description: Theuth presents writing as an aid to memory and intelligence. Thamus challenges the inventor's assessment and distinguishes reminders from understanding.

whyItMatters.title: Desire and understanding
whyItMatters.body: The dialogue asks whether love distracts people from truth or can lead them toward it. Its contrasting speeches let the reader compare competing accounts rather than encounter a single uninterrupted doctrine.

whyItMatters.title: The responsibilities of persuasion
whyItMatters.body: Socrates asks what a speaker must understand before trying to convince anyone. His examples give readers a way to examine the relationship between knowledge, audience and technique.

whyItMatters.title: Reading as a starting point
whyItMatters.body: The critique of writing distinguishes possessing words from understanding them. It encourages a reader to question, explain and defend an idea rather than simply repeat it.
